title: Whole Turkey (frozen)

drivers.name: Price increase (2.9%)
drivers.evidence: Same price in 2026-04-06–2026-04-20: sales averaged 4.0, below baseline (5.1). Last year’s same-week price (28.37) saw 4.0 units. Price rise correlates with lower sales. No promotion history supports lift at this price.

adjustment.analysis: The baseline median is 5.1. No events are scheduled for the target week. The price is raised by 2.9% vs regular, which historically suppresses demand. Past promotions show noise-adjusted lift of x1.0, indicating no reliable uplift. The week after Easter (2026-04-06) saw 5 units at the same price—consistent with baseline. The prior week (2026-04-20) sold only 2 units, suggesting a downward trend. Mother’s Day (2024) had a noise-adjusted lift of x1.0. The price increase is a clear demand reducer; no evidence supports a promotion or event. The classical model’s x1.0 is correct, but price impact is real and unmodeled. Adjust down slightly.

PRODUCT: Whole Turkey (frozen) | category Meat | Store #12 (Austin, TX)
TARGET WEEK: 2026-04-27 to 2026-05-03 (next week)

KNOWN PLAN FOR THE TARGET WEEK:
  events: none
  shelf price: 29.20 (+2.9% vs regular price 28.37)

STATISTICAL BASELINE (exponential smoothing of recent sales; it ignores events, promotions and prices):
  median 5.1 | 5%-95%: 0.0 - 17.0 | 10%-90%: 0.4 - 12.0

In the evidence below, 'vs baseline' = actual units / what this same baseline predicted for that week.
It is the multiplier that would have been right, so it maps directly onto median_multiplier.
This product's ordinary weeks already swing about +/-101% around the baseline, so a past effect smaller than that, seen only a few times, is mostly noise. The
'noise-adjusted estimate' is the effect shrunk toward x1.0 for that noise and the number of sightings.
